title: Gram-Negative First Forks: Oxidase, Neisseria Sugars, X and V, HACEK
summary: Use the oxidase test to separate the Enterobacteriaceae from oxidase-positive gram-negatives, identify Neisseria by sugar use, Haemophilus by X and V factors, and grow HACEK organisms correctly.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hits 10, 11, 13, 28 and 43. Checked against the WHO/CDC 2003 manual (Perilla et al.), the CDC 1998 meningitis laboratory manual and Khaledi 2022. Hit 36 calls HACEK “culture-negative”; Khaledi 2022 reports ~99% detection within 5 days by an automated system and no value for prolonged incubation (register flag rv-hacek-culture). Not taught: HACEK failing to grow on MacConkey (Trap 5), the Pseudomonas grape odour and sneaker-puncture association (Hits 24, 26), Hib epidemiology, and indole for E. coli vs Klebsiella (not in the sources read).

objectives: Perform and read the Kovac’s oxidase test and name oxidase-positive and oxidase-negative groups.
Identify N. meningitidis, N. gonorrhoeae and related species by carbohydrate use, with the gonococcal caveat.
Identify H. influenzae by X and V requirements, media and satellitism, and separate it from H. haemolyticus and H. parainfluenzae.
Describe growth conditions and blood-culture detection of HACEK organisms.

scenes.title: Three gram-negatives, three first questions
scenes.altText: Three isolate cards. Isolate A: tiny gram-negative coccobacilli from a toddler’s CSF; grows on chocolate agar but not sheep blood agar. Isolate B: gram-negative diplococci from a urethral swab on modified Thayer–Martin. Isolate C: gram-negative rods from stool; a swab of the colony turns purple within seconds of adding oxidase reagent. A question token: “Which one test sorts each?” The cartoon scientist holds an oxidase swab.

cues.text: Isolate A: tiny gram-negative coccobacilli from a toddler’s spinal fluid. They grow on chocolate agar but not on sheep blood agar.
Isolate B: gram-negative diplococci from a urethral swab, growing on modified Thayer–Martin.
Isolate C: gram-negative rods from stool that turn an oxidase swab purple within seconds. Three organisms; each has one sorting test that matters most.

scenes.title: The oxidase test: one swab, one fork
scenes.altText: A swab with a colony picked from a non-selective plate; a drop of Kovac’s reagent (1% tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine). Cytochrome c oxidase turns it purple — a positive must appear within 10 seconds. A note: the dimethyl (Gordon–McLeod) reagent turns blue and takes 10–30 minutes. Two bins: oxidase-positive — Vibrio, Neisseria, Campylobacter, Aeromonas, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas, Alcaligenes; oxidase-negative — all Enterobacteriaceae (Enterobacterales), e.g., E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella.

cues.text: The oxidase test asks one question: does the organism have cytochrome c oxidase in its respiratory chain? Pick a colony from a non-selective plate.
Add Kovac’s reagent, tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine. A positive turns purple, and it must do so within 10 seconds. Later colour does not count.
Some labs use the dimethyl reagent instead. It turns blue, and slowly, over 10 to 30 minutes.
Oxidase-positive: Vibrio, Neisseria, Campylobacter, Aeromonas, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas and Alcaligenes.
Oxidase-negative: every member of the Enterobacteriaceae, such as E. coli, Salmonella and Shigella. A positive result rules them out.

scenes.title: Neisseria: which sugars turn yellow
scenes.altText: A row of CTA sugar tubes (schematic): glucose, maltose, lactose, sucrose. N. meningitidis: glucose + maltose. N. gonorrhoeae: glucose only, and weak — some strains look glucose-negative. N. lactamica: glucose + maltose + lactose. N. sicca: glucose + maltose + sucrose. Moraxella catarrhalis: none. A caution card: do not read a tube negative before 72 hours; confirm gonococci with additional tests because weak acid producers can look glucose-negative.

cues.text: Neisseria are oxidase-positive diplococci, so the next fork is sugar use, classically in cystine trypticase agar. A yellow tube means acid.
Meningococcus uses glucose and maltose. Gonococcus uses glucose only.
Neisseria lactamica adds lactose, Neisseria sicca adds sucrose, and Moraxella catarrhalis uses none of them.
Watch gonococcus: its acid production is weak, so some strains look glucose-negative. A negative gonococcal result is not reliable on its own.
Do not call a tube negative before 72 hours, and back up a gonococcal identification with additional tests.

scenes.title: Haemophilus factors and the HACEK group
scenes.altText: A chocolate plate and a sheep blood plate: H. influenzae grows on chocolate (heated blood frees X = hemin and V = NAD) but not on plain sheep blood agar — unless the sheep blood plate is cross-streaked with S. aureus, along which satellite colonies form. A disk test on factor-free medium: growth only around the XV disk. Table: H. influenzae X+ V+, non-hemolytic; H. haemolyticus X+ V+, β-hemolytic on rabbit or horse blood; H. parainfluenzae V only. A HACEK card: oral and upper-respiratory flora, slow-growing, enhanced by 5–10% CO₂ on blood and chocolate agar; automated blood cultures detect ~99% within 5 days, so prolonged incubation adds little. Back to the hook: A = Haemophilus (confirm X and V), B = Neisseria (sugars), C = oxidase-positive, not an enteric.

cues.text: Haemophilus influenzae grows on chocolate agar, where heated blood releases X factor, hemin, and V factor, NAD. Plain sheep blood agar does not support it.
Unless you cross-streak the sheep blood plate with Staphylococcus aureus. Tiny satellite colonies then grow along the staph streak.

On factor-free medium with paper disks, H. influenzae grows only around the disk with both X and V. H. haemolyticus needs both too, but it is beta-hemolytic on rabbit or horse blood. H. parainfluenzae needs V only.
The HACEK group are slow-growing oral and upper-respiratory flora that grow better in 5 to 10 percent carbon dioxide. Automated blood cultures detect about 99 percent within five days.
So isolate A is Haemophilus: confirm X and V. Isolate B is Neisseria: check the sugars. Isolate C is oxidase-positive, so it is not an enteric.

scenes.title: Four classic traps
scenes.altText: Four trap cards: “Oxidase purple after 2 minutes with Kovac’s = positive” (✓ only within 10 seconds counts); “Glucose-negative CTA rules out gonococcus” (✓ weak acid producers can look negative — confirm); “Growth around the XV disk = H. influenzae” (✓ or H. haemolyticus — check hemolysis on rabbit or horse blood); “Suspected HACEK: incubate blood cultures for weeks” (✓ ~99% detected within 5 days in automated systems).

cues.text: Trap one: oxidase purple after two minutes with Kovac’s reagent is positive. No. Only a colour within 10 seconds counts.
Trap two: a glucose-negative CTA tube rules out gonococcus. Weak acid producers can look negative. Confirm with other tests.
Trap three: growth only around the XV disk means H. influenzae. It could be H. haemolyticus. Check hemolysis on rabbit or horse blood.
Trap four: hold blood cultures for weeks to find HACEK. Automated systems detect about 99 percent within five days.

Where it breaks: the dimethyl reagent turns blue and takes longer; weak gonococci can look glucose-negative; and H. haemolyticus also needs X and V.

cues.text: Oxidase splits gram-negatives from the enterics, sugars split the Neisseria, X and V factors identify Haemophilus influenzae, and HACEK grow with extra carbon dioxide within five days.

props.label: Oxidase ≤ 10 s: + Vibrio · Neisseria · Campylobacter · Pseudomonas · − Enterobacteriaceae

explanation.what: Plain language: a few quick tests tell gram-negative bacteria apart — whether they turn an oxidase reagent purple, which sugars they use and which blood-derived growth factors they need. Scientific terms: cytochrome c oxidase, Kovac’s (tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine) reagent, cystine trypticase agar (CTA), X factor (hemin), V factor (NAD), satellitism, HACEK (Haemophilus [Aggregatibacter], Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella).
explanation.why: Oxidase-positive organisms carry cytochrome c in their respiratory chain; the Enterobacteriaceae do not. Neisseria species differ in which sugars they oxidize to acid. H. influenzae cannot make hemin or NAD; chocolate agar’s heated blood releases both, and S. aureus colonies supply V factor on sheep blood agar.
explanation.measure: Kovac’s oxidase: purple within 10 s (dimethyl reagent: blue in 10–30 min). CTA: do not read negative before 72 h. X/V disks on factor-free medium, CO₂, 35 °C, 18–24 h. HACEK: blood and chocolate agar in 5–10% CO₂; automated blood cultures ~99% sensitive within 5 days.
explanation.differs: N. meningitidis (glucose + maltose) vs N. gonorrhoeae (glucose only, weak) vs N. lactamica (+ lactose) vs M. catarrhalis (none). H. influenzae (X + V, non-hemolytic) vs H. haemolyticus (X + V, β-hemolytic) vs H. parainfluenzae (V only). Oxidase-positive gram-negative rods vs Enterobacteriaceae (oxidase-negative).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: oxidase-positive vs Enterobacterales, gonococcus vs meningococcus sugars, X and V factor patterns and satellitism, and HACEK growth needs.

questions.stem: A CSF isolate of small gram-negative coccobacilli grows on factor-free agar only around the disk containing both X and V factors and is non-hemolytic on rabbit blood agar. What is the identification?

options.rationale: Correct. Requires X and V and is non-hemolytic on rabbit blood.
Incorrect. It also needs X and V but is β-hemolytic on rabbit or horse blood.
Incorrect. It needs V factor only and would grow around the V disk.
Incorrect. Meningococci are diplococci that grow on sheep blood agar without added factors.

questions.stem: Oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococci from CSF produce acid from glucose and maltose but not lactose or sucrose. What is the most likely organism?

options.rationale: Correct. Glucose + maltose is the meningococcal pattern.
Incorrect. N. lactamica also uses lactose.
Incorrect. M. catarrhalis produces acid from none of these sugars.

questions.stem: A technologist adds Kovac’s oxidase reagent to a colony on a swab. No colour appears at 10 seconds, but the swab is faintly purple at 2 minutes. How should the result be recorded?

options.rationale: Correct. With Kovac’s reagent, only a purple colour within 10 seconds counts as positive.
Incorrect. Late colour with Kovac’s reagent is not a positive result.
Incorrect. Enterobacteriaceae are oxidase-negative; there is no “weak positive” category here.

options.text: Repeat with the dimethyl reagent and read at 10 seconds
options.rationale: Incorrect. The dimethyl reagent is slower (10–30 minutes).

claims.text: Kovac’s oxidase purple within 10 s (dimethyl blue 10–30 min); oxidase-positive Vibrio, Neisseria, Campylobacter, Aeromonas, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas, Alcaligenes; Enterobacteriaceae negative.
CTA sugar patterns for Neisseria and M. catarrhalis; weak gonococci may look glucose-negative; no negative before 72 h.
H. influenzae requires X and V; chocolate not sheep blood; satellites along S. aureus; XV disk only; H. haemolyticus β-hemolytic; H. parainfluenzae V only.
HACEK oral/upper-respiratory flora, slow, enhanced by 5–10% CO₂; ~99% detected within 5 days by automated blood culture.
HACEK do not grow on MacConkey; Pseudomonas grape odour and sneaker puncture osteomyelitis; indole separates E. coli from Klebsiella.
